title: Samsung and SK Hynix Race for ASML’s Scarce EUV Machines
author: B
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Samsung and SK Hynix are racing to secure the machines that will help determine how quickly they can expand advanced memory production.

Both companies are reportedly committing approximately $6.7 billion to $13.3 billion each to ASML’s extreme ultraviolet lithography equipment. With equipment lead times reportedly doubling, they are also considering placing future orders earlier to secure delivery slots.

SK Hynix has already disclosed an equipment purchase worth approximately $8 billion, with delivery scheduled by December 31, 2027. Samsung, meanwhile, has reportedly ordered lithography equipment for its Pyeongtaek P5 development, where investment is expected to exceed approximately $40 billion per fab.

The supply constraint is real. ASML said in its October results that its currently planned capacity would not fully satisfy customer demand in either 2027 or 2028. It is exploring additional expansion beyond its previously discussed capacity increases.

Why does this matter? My assessment is that delivery timing is becoming a competitive advantage. A chipmaker can finance a new factory and complete its cleanroom, but production still depends on having the necessary equipment installed, qualified, and running reliably.

For Samsung and SK Hynix, securing those machines earlier could help protect technology roadmaps, accelerate capacity additions, and strengthen their ability to serve customers. Delays could leave expensive infrastructure waiting for tools while competitors move ahead.

The implications extend to AI infrastructure. Equipment shortages could influence how quickly additional memory supply reaches the market, although yields, packaging capacity, and customer qualification will also shape the outcome.

There is a financial tradeoff, too. Ordering earlier requires companies to commit capital further ahead of actual production needs, increasing exposure if demand changes.

The strategic question is becoming clear: who can turn enormous spending commitments into qualified production capacity first?
